Gödel’s Continuum Papers, Complete and Corrected in His Own Hand

GÖDEL, Kurt.

The Consistency of the Axiom of Choice and of the Generalized Continuum-Hypothesis. [With:] Consistency-Proof for the Generalized Continuum-Hypothesis. [With:] What is Cantor’s Continuum Problem?

Washington, D.C., & Lancaster, PA: National Academy of Sciences; Mathematical Association of America, 1938–1947.

First edition, first-printing offprints — all three of the papers in which Gödel resolved half of the oldest open question in the theory of the infinite, here in the copies of the physicist Abraham Pais, each carrying corrections in Gödel’s own hand. In two pages of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences for December 1938, in five for April 1939, and in the American Mathematical Monthly essay of November 1947, Gödel announced, then proved, that the Axiom of Choice and the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis cannot be disproved from the axioms of set theory — building, to do it, the ‘constructible universe’ that has organised the subject ever since — and then, having shown the hypothesis irrefutable, argued that it is nonetheless probably false. No other surviving form gathers the announcement, the proof, and the reconsideration in a single set; this one gathers them corrected in the author’s hand, and is itself one of the two independently-descended copies by which those corrections are established as his.

The question was Cantor’s. Having shown in the 1870s that the infinity of the real numbers strictly exceeds that of the integers, he conjectured that nothing lies between the two — that the continuum is the very next magnitude of infinity after the countable. He could neither prove the conjecture nor let it go, and when Hilbert drew up the twenty-three problems he set before the new century in 1900, the continuum hypothesis stood first on the list. Little of substance was added for nearly four decades, until the three papers gathered here.

The earliest of them, the two-page note of December 1938, is the first public word on the result and the first appearance in print of the constructible universe itself. Gödel states his theorem — that if the axioms of set theory without the Axiom of Choice are consistent, they remain so when Choice and the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis are adjoined — and describes, without yet proving, the model that does the work: the ‘mathematically constructible’ sets, built through Russell’s ramified hierarchy of types extended into the transfinite, in which the proposition he labels A, that every set is constructible, holds. The note closes on a sentence read and re-read ever since: that A ‘seems to give a natural completion of the axioms of set theory,’ and that the consistency proof does not break down if stronger axioms of infinity — ‘the existence of inaccessible numbers’ — are adjoined. In two clauses Gödel had pointed at both of the directions twentieth-century set theory would take: the axiom of constructibility, today written V = L, and the large cardinals that reach beyond it. He was then inclined to believe A true; he would change his mind entirely in the third paper of this set.

The note of April 1939 is the first published proof. Here Gödel defines the constructible sets Mα by transfinite recursion, builds the hierarchy whose union is the inner model later denoted L, and shows in eight numbered theorems that within it the axioms of set theory hold together with Choice and with the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis. Robert Solovay, introducing the papers in Gödel’s Collected Works, treats this note as the conceptual heart of the consistency result and bases his own exposition ‘substantially’ upon it; Akihiro Kanamori observes that in it Gödel ‘presented L essentially as is done today.’ The constructible model first drawn in these five pages is the inner model against which the rest of set theory still defines itself — the fine structure later read off it by Ronald Jensen organises the subject’s hardest combinatorics, and the discovery that a single large cardinal forces the universe to outrun L (Dana Scott, 1961) is the exact sense in which it marks the lower boundary of the set-theoretic world.

The third paper is the one that makes the set a complete intellectual record. In ‘What is Cantor’s Continuum Problem?’ (1947) Gödel set out, for a wider readership, what the continuum hypothesis is and what his consistency proof had and had not shown — and then went further than the technical notes ever had. Holding that the objects of set theory exist independently of our constructions, he argued that the hypothesis must be either true or false in that reality whatever the present axioms can decide, that the axioms are therefore incomplete, and that one should expect the hypothesis to be false: many plausible propositions imply its negation while none implies it, so that the continuum problem should lead, he wrote, to ‘the discovery of new axioms which will make it possible to disprove Cantor’s conjecture.’ It is also, and not incidentally, the paper whose footnote sets out the notational corrections that stand in Gödel’s hand in the 1939 note bound with it here — so that this set holds, in one place, both the proof and the published instruction for its own emendation.

The corrections are the author’s second thoughts, entered at the points he later made public. On the 1938 leaf two stand in pencil: in the Theorem the parenthetical ‘(Ax. III 3*)’ is struck, with a marginal note in his Latin cursive — ‘i.e. replacing Ax. III 3* by Ax. III 3’ — and, in the equation of the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis, the subscript dropped by the printer from the exponent aleph is supplied by hand. In the 1939 note the letter α, which the printing had set both for the running ordinal of the constructible hierarchy and for the distinct cardinal index in the bounding argument of pp. 221–223, is corrected to μ wherever the two had collided, with the sign ≡ supplied in Theorem 6 — exactly the emendations Gödel published over his own name in the 1947 essay. The third paper carries further pencil marginalia to its definitions pages. None of the marks is cosmetic: each disentangles a symbol the printing had run together, and the supplied 1938 subscript and the 1939 μ are the difference between a proof that reads consistently and one that does not.

That the correcting hand is Gödel’s rests on more than the few letters. The decisive mark is the supplied subscript on the 1938 leaf: it was never issued as an erratum and is recorded in no edition of the Collected Works, which prints the equation correct without remark — so there exists no source from which a later reader could have copied it. The same correction, in the same hand, stands in a second set of these offprints descended through an entirely separate line: the copies preserved in the working library of the Berkeley Group in Logic and the Methodology of Science, the programme built around Alfred Tarski. Two readers each following Gödel’s printed instructions might write the same letter in the same place, but not in the same hand; agreement at the level of the stroke between two independently-descended copies can descend only from a single corrector. A formal comparison of the correcting hand against dated specimens of Gödel’s autograph found nothing to set against the identification. The marks are thus Gödel’s own corrections, present in manuscript and corroborated by an independent copy — the strongest footing short of a signed statement.

The provenance is exact and distinguished. Each of the three offprints is signed ‘Pais’ at the head. Abraham Pais (1918–2000), the Dutch-American physicist, came to the Institute for Advanced Study in 1946 and was its professor of physics until 1963 — the years of his work in particle physics and, later, of the biographies of Einstein and Bohr by which he is now also widely known. Pais and Gödel were colleagues at the Institute for some seventeen years; by Pais’s own account he walked Einstein home from the Institute at lunchtime in Gödel’s company. The offprints passed by the natural route of that milieu, presumably from the author directly to a colleague who would keep them — and keep them corrected.

Gödel published little, and his offprints are uncommon in commerce at any date; a copy bearing his working corrections belongs to a further order of scarcity, and a complete set of all three continuum papers so corrected, with a named provenance, has no parallel we can trace. What these marks preserve is not a presentation courtesy but the labour behind the proof — the author returning to his published pages, pen in hand, to set right the symbols the printing had run together, across the announcement, the proof, and the essay that prescribed the corrections. The question the three papers opened did not close until 1963, when Paul Cohen’s method of forcing — set out in Set Theory and the Continuum Hypothesis (1966) — produced models in which the continuum hypothesis fails; Gödel’s constructible universe and Cohen’s forcing are the two halves of a single answer, and the hypothesis is independent of the axioms — the negative solution to the first of Hilbert’s problems. The constructible hierarchy first drawn in these pages remained, and remains, the indispensable instrument. The present set is that achievement entire, in the copies its author kept correcting.

References Gödel, ‘The consistency of the axiom of choice and of the generalized continuum-hypothesis’ (1938), ‘Consistency-proof for the generalized continuum-hypothesis’ (1939a), and ‘What is Cantor’s continuum problem?’, American Mathematical Monthly 54 (1947), pp. 515–525 — with Solovay’s introductory note and the textual notes — in Feferman, Dawson, Kleene, Moore, Solovay and van Heijenoort (eds.), Kurt Gödel: Collected Works, vol. II: Publications 1938–1974 (Oxford: Clarendon, 1990) — Feferman, ‘Gödel’s life and work’, in Collected Works, vol. I (Clarendon, 1986) — Kanamori, ‘Gödel and set theory’, Bulletin of Symbolic Logic 13 (2007), pp. 153–188 — Dawson, Logical Dilemmas: The Life and Work of Kurt Gödel (A. K. Physical description

Three offprints, each reprinted from its journal of first publication. I. ‘The Consistency of the Axiom of Choice and of the Generalized Continuum-Hypothesis’, from the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 24, no. 12 (December 1938); large 8vo (258 × 174 mm), pp. [556]–557, a single self-contained leaf, issued without wrappers. II. ‘Consistency-Proof for the Generalized Continuum-Hypothesis’, from ibid. 25, no. 4 (April 1939); large 8vo (258 × 174 mm), pp. 220–224, in the original tan printed wrapper. III. ‘What is Cantor’s Continuum Problem?’, from the American Mathematical Monthly 54, no. 9 (November 1947); 8vo (253 × 182 mm), pp. 515–525, in the original blue printed wrapper. Each signed ‘Pais’ in the upper outer corner of its first leaf or wrapper. Manuscript corrections in pencil in Gödel’s hand: on the 1938 leaf, ‘(Ax. III 3*)’ struck in the Theorem with the lower-margin note ‘i.e. replacing Ax. III 3* by Ax. III 3’, and the α subscript supplied to the exponent aleph in the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis equation; in the 1939 paper, α corrected to μ at the points later specified in Gödel’s 1947 erratum, through pp. 221–223, with the sign ≡ supplied in Theorem 6 on p. 222 and marginal μ reminders. The 1947 paper bears further pencil marginalia to its definitions pages (pp. 524–525). Light handling only; the wrappers clean and unfaded, the 1938 leaf sound. Fine copies.
